title: Mother, I didn't eat the butter
hookLine: a husband scolded by his wife, and a singer remembered as blind who saw a toddler covered in butter
carry: dasya and vatsalya: God as king, God as child
tomorrow: why does a whole street sing the same names?

lines: IF YOU LOVED RAMA HALF AS MUCH.
HE GAVE HIS LIFE TO RAMA.
cards: The story goes that a young man named Tulsi loved his wife so much he couldn't bear a single night apart.
Once, when she'd gone to visit her parents, he followed her through a storm, across a flooded river, and climbed up to her window. She was not charmed.
She told him, more or less: all this passion for a body of flesh and bone. If you had half of it for Rama, you'd be free. It stung.
He left, and gave the rest of his life to Rama. Whether or not it happened just like that, what he wrote next is why his name is still known.

teach.h: THE LAKE OF THE DEEDS OF RAMA.
teach.b: Tulsidas retold the Ramayana. Not in Sanskrit, but in Awadhi, a language ordinary people in the Hindi heartland actually spoke. He called it the Ramcharitmanas, the lake of the deeds of Rama.

In autumn, towns and villages act it out as the Ramlila, and families read it aloud at home. The Hanuman Chalisa, a prayer to Hanuman often recited on Tuesdays and Saturdays, is traditionally credited to him too.
His love is a servant's: dasya, the seventh of the nine forms. Rama is the king, and Tulsidas is his servant, happy to be. Now a very different voice.

Surdas, a poet remembered by tradition as blind, sang in Braj, the language of Krishna's country, and the Krishna he saw was mostly a small child. One song sung in his name is a toddler talking to his mother.
Maiya mori, main nahin makhan khayo.

teach.h: MOTHER, I DIDN'T EAT THE BUTTER.
teach.b: Mother, I didn't eat the butter. Then the excuses: the other boys smeared it on my face. My arms are too short to reach the pot.
And Yashoda, his mother, laughing, gathers him up.
That's vatsalya: a parent's love for a child, aimed at God. Here God is the kid with butter on his face, lying badly, and you're the one who loves him anyway. Two poets, two kinds of love.

teach.h: GOD AS KING, GOD AS CHILD.
teach.b: The servant bowing to the king. The mother catching the thief. That parent's love is why some Hindu homes care for a small image of baby Krishna like a child, even putting him to bed at night.

how: Across North India, families read Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas aloud and watch it performed in the autumn Ramlila, the Hanuman Chalisa is often recited on Tuesdays and Saturdays, and Surdas's songs of child Krishna are sung as bhajans, especially around Janmashtami.

loving God as a servant would, or as a parent loves a child

games.q: you're Yashoda. your little boy has butter all over his face and swears the other boys smeared it on him. in Surdas's song, what happens?
o: she laughs and gathers him up.
she believes him and scolds the other boys.
games.why: she laughs and holds him. Surdas's bhakti is vatsalya, a parent's love, aimed at God.

practice: Try on two kinds of love. First the servant's: think of someone, or something, you'd gladly serve, and notice what it's like to bow a little.
Then the parent's: picture a small child, one you know or the one you were, caught in a sweet, bad lie, and notice which love softens you more.

wordCard.voice: Bhakti yoga, through Tulsidas and Surdas. Tulsidas loved Rama as a servant loves a king; Surdas loved child Krishna as a mother loves a toddler caught with the butter.

carryVoice: Your line: dasya and vatsalya, God as king, God as child. A servant's bow and a mother's laugh both travel the road. Day two seventy-two, complete.
